what_its_for: Cephalexin is an antibiotic used to treat bacterial infections. It is commonly prescribed for skin infections, ear infections, urinary tract infections (UTIs), throat infections (strep throat), and bone infections. It works by killing the bacteria causing your infection. It does NOT work for viral infections like the cold or flu.
how_to_take: Take cephalexin by mouth with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, taking it with food or milk may help. Swallow the capsule or tablet whole with a full glass of water. If you have liquid cephalexin, shake the bottle well before each use and measure your dose carefully with the measuring spoon or cup that came with it. Take all of your medication even if you start feeling better. Stopping early can allow the infection to come back or become harder to treat.
dosing: Your doctor will tell you your exact dose. The usual adult dose is 250 mg to 500 mg taken every 6 to 12 hours, depending on your infection. Most courses last 7 to 14 days. Always follow your doctor's or pharmacist's instructions and do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do NOT take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one, as this can increase your risk of side effects.
storage: Store cephalexin capsules or tablets at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep them in a closed container. Store liquid cephalexin in the refrigerator — do NOT freeze it. Liquid cephalexin must be thrown away after 14 days, even if there is some left. Keep all medications out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid skipping doses or stopping the medication early, even if you feel better. Avoid taking antacids that contain aluminum or magnesium within 2 hours of your dose, as they may reduce how well cephalexin works. Avoid drinking large amounts of alcohol, as it can increase side effects like stomach upset. Tell your doctor if you are taking metformin, blood thinners like warfarin, or probenecid, as these may interact with cephalexin.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: a severe allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of your face, lips, tongue or throat, or trouble breathing; a severe skin rash or blistering; severe or watery diarrhea that does not stop (this could be a serious gut infection called C. difficile); yellowing of your skin or eyes; dark urine; seizures; or if your infection does not seem to be getting better after a few days of treatment.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 2 to 3 days of starting cephalexin. However, it is very important to keep taking all of your doses until the prescription is finished, even if your symptoms go away. If you do not feel any improvement after 3 days, or if your symptoms get worse, contact your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults and people with kidney disease may need a lower dose because their kidneys may not clear the medication as quickly. Cephalexin is generally considered safe to use during pregnancy and while breastfeeding, but always tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children can take cephalexin, but the dose is based on their weight, so follow your doctor's instructions carefully. If your child is using the liquid form, make sure you are using the correct measuring device.
